This PR adds the `scraperID` to the error logs for scrapers (metrics, logs, and profiles). Why is this important?

issue.title: [otelcol] components command hides components that have deprecated type aliases
issue.body:
### Component(s)

otelcol

### What happened?

**Describe the bug**  
`otelcol components` omits *canonical* component types when the component factory exposes a deprecated type alias (e.g., snake_case rename with legacy alias). This makes the command misleading: the component works in config, but it doesn’t appear in the `components` output. This seems related to the alias handling used/introduced around PR #14493

**Steps to reproduce**  
1. <your-otelcol-binary> components | grep -nE 'k8s_attributes|k8sattributes'
2.  nothing comes out of the output while it did until version 0.145.0

**What did you expect to see?**  
The canonical component (`k8s_attributes`) should still be present in `otelcol components` output. (Aliases can be shown separately/as metadata, but canonical should not disappear.)

**What did you see instead?**  
The canonical factory is filtered out because `sortFactoriesByType` excludes anything for which `isComponentAlias(...)` returns true, and `isComponentAlias` currently returns true whenever `DeprecatedAlias() != ""`. As a result, `otelcol components` output can miss canonical components that have deprecated aliases.

### Collector version

0.146.0/0.146.1/0.147.0

issue.title: [pdata] pCommon.Value.AsString function escapes HTML on ValueTypeMap and ValueTypeSlice
issue.body:
### Component(s)

pdata

### What happened?

**Describe the bug**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->
There is a misalignment on how Value.AsString works with value of string type and values of map and slice.
HTML escaping is not done for strings but done for map and slices. 
For instance, "<".ToString() -> "<" but ["<"].ToString() -> ["\u003c"] and {"key": "<"}.ToString()
-> {"key": "\u003c"}.

We should make map and slice to not escape HTML as well so 
["<"].ToString() -> ["<"] and {"key": "<"}.ToString() -> {"key": "<"}.

The issue is https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/pdata/pcommon/value.go#L404 and https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/pdata/pcommon/value.go#L411 uses Go's encoding/json which escapes HTML when Marshalling. 

**Steps to reproduce**
<!-- If possible, provide a recipe for reproducing the error. -->
1. Configure the collector with a receiver and exporter that uses pdata.
2. Send an event whose body is of type map or slice and contains "<" ">" or "&"
3.  See the exported event body contains escaped HTML.

**What did you expect to see?**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what you expected to see. -->
Nothing should be escaped.
"<".AsString() -> "<" | ["<"].AsString() -> ["<"] | {"key": "<"}.AsString() -> {"key": "<"}.

**What did you see instead?**
<!-- A clear and concise description of what you saw instead. -->
"<".AsString() -> "<" but ["<"].AsString() -> ["\u003c"] and {"key": "<"}.AsString()
-> {"key": "\u003c"}.

### Collector version

v1.52.0

### Environment information

OS: (e.g., "Ubuntu 20.04")
Compiler(if manually compiled): (e.g., "go 14.2")

```yaml

```


prompt.pr_body:
## Description

`pcommon.Value.AsString` uses `json.Marshal` for `ValueTypeMap` and `ValueTypeSlice`, which HTML-escapes `<`, `>`, and `&` into `\u003c`, `\u003e`, and `\u0026`. This is inconsistent with `ValueTypeStr`, which returns the raw string, and corrupts structured log bodies whose content happens to contain those characters.

```
"<".AsString()       -> "<"
["<"].AsString()     -> ["\u003c"]   // surprising
{"key":"<"}.AsString() -> {"key":"\u003c"} // surprising
```

Switch to `json.Encoder` with `SetEscapeHTML(false)` so that maps and slices serialize the same way strings do.

Closes #14662

## Link to tracking Issue
#14662

## Testing

Added `map_with_html_characters` and `slice_with_html_characters` sub-tests to `TestValueAsString`. `go test ./pcommon/... -run TestValueAsString` passes (14/14).

## Documentation

.chloggen entry added.

issue.title: Shared receiver can start serving before consumers of its   other-signal pipelines are started
issue.body:
### Component(s)

service

### What happened?

**Describe the bug**

If you share one OTLP receiver across pipelines of different signals (say one `otlp` receiver feeding traces, logs and metrics), the order in which components start is not deterministic between those pipelines.
And since the OTLP receiver is a sharedcomponent, whichever per-signal receiver node happens to start first brings up the single HTTP/gRPC server for all signals at once.
So the server can start accepting data for a signal whose pipeline hasn't finished starting yet.

I'm fairly sure this is what's actually behind the k8sattributes startup panic in [contrib #47672][contrib-47672] (`processor.go:202`).
k8sattributes only sets its kube client (`kc`, an interface) in `Start()`.
If a span arrives before that `Start()` has run, `kc` is still nil and the call dispatches on a nil interface.

The usual "reverse-topological start guarantees consumers are up before the receiver" reasoning holds, but only inside a single connected pipeline.
It doesn't carry across signals for a shared receiver, because the graph doesn't treat that receiver as one node.

Here's the chain as I read it:

- A shared receiver gets one node *per signal*, not one node total. The node ID comes from `(signal, componentID)` (see `newReceiverNode` in `service/internal/graph/receiver.go`). With a different exporter per signal, the per-signal subgraphs end up disconnected from each other:

  ```
  recv[traces] -> proc[traces] -> exp[traces]
  recv[logs]   -> proc[logs]   -> exp[logs]
  recv[metrics]-> proc[metrics]-> exp[metrics]
  ```

- `StartAll` does `topo.Sort(componentGraph)` and starts in reverse order (`service/internal/graph/graph.go`). gonum keeps the nodes in a map, so the sort doesn't fix any relative order *between* the disconnected subgraphs. There's no barrier or two-phase "start everything, then serve".

- The single server registers handlers for every signal at build time, not at start time (otlpreceiver's `startHTTPServer` wires `/v1/traces`, `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/logs` together). So the first receiver node to start opens the door for all three.

Put together: reverse-topo does guarantee `recv[traces]` starts after the traces processors, but the server isn't tied to `recv[traces]` — it's brought up by whichever signal's node wins the race.
If that's `recv[logs]` and the traces pipeline's k8sattributes `Start()` hasn't run, a request comes in, gets routed into a chain whose `kc` is still nil, and you hit `processor.go:202`.

Worth noting it's not specific to traces.
`processResource` is shared by processTraces/Logs/Metrics/Profiles, so a cluster sending only logs and metrics can crash the same way.
The victim is just whichever shared-receiver-fed pipeline hasn't been started yet when the server goes live.

**Steps to reproduce**

I wrote a small test — [startorder_race_test.go](https://github.com/tank-500m/opentelemetry-collector/blob/test/sharedreceiver-startorder-race/service/internal/graph/startorder_race_test.go) — that builds a real graph through `graph.Build()` (one `examplereceiver` shared by a traces and a logs pipeline) and then runs `topo.Sort` on the resulting `componentGraph` the same way `StartAll` does.
The graph isn't hand-built; the nodes, per-signal IDs and edges all come from the builder.
It just counts how often the receiver's logs node ends up starting before the traces processor.

```
$ go test -v -count=3 -run TestSharedReceiverStartOrderIsNonDeterministic ./service/internal/graph/
=== RUN   TestSharedReceiverStartOrderIsNonDeterministic
    startorder_race_test.go: iters=5000  panic-window(recvLogs<procTraces)=972   safe=4028
--- PASS
=== RUN   TestSharedReceiverStartOrderIsNonDeterministic
    startorder_race_test.go: iters=5000  panic-window(recvLogs<procTraces)=997   safe=4003
--- PASS
=== RUN   TestSharedReceiverStartOrderIsNonDeterministic
    startorder_race_test.go: iters=5000  panic-window(recvLogs<procTraces)=1031  safe=3969
--- PASS
```

I also reproduced the actual crash end to end.
Built a collector with an `otlp` (gRPC) receiver, k8sattributes and a debug exporter, with the one receiver shared across traces/logs/metrics (separate exporter per signal).
The kube client never syncs (`KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` points at an unreachable address), so `kc` only becomes non-nil once `Start()` runs.
The only code change is a delay at the very top of k8sattributes' `Start()`, gated on an env var so it's a no-op normally.
The panic line itself is untouched; the delay just widens the `kc == nil` window (it's microseconds in practice) enough for in-flight traffic to land in it:

```go
// processor/k8sattributesprocessor/processor.go, first lines of Start()
if d := os.Getenv("K8SATTR_START_DELAY"); d != "" {
    if delay, err := time.ParseDuration(d); err == nil && delay > 0 {
        time.Sleep(delay) // widen the window before kp.kc is set; no-op when unset
    }
}
```

With that I get the panic (gRPC doesn't recover per request, so the process just dies), and the victim signal moves around between logs/metrics/traces run to run:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
...k8sattributesprocessor.(*kubernetesprocessor).processResource(...)
    processor/k8sattributesprocessor/processor.go:218   // kp.kc.GetPod(...)
...processTraces(...) -> processorhelper -> otlpreceiver Export
google.golang.org/grpc.(*Server).processUnaryRPC(...)
```

For what it's worth, turning on the `ShareProcessorBetweenPipelines` feature gate made the crash go away (0/30 under the same setup): with a single shared processor instance, its `Start()` (and the `kc` assignment) runs before any receiver node brings the server up.
That only works when every fed pipeline uses the same processor id, though.

**What did you expect to see?**

A shared receiver shouldn't start serving a signal until the consumers of every pipeline it feeds are up — including the pipelines for other signals, not just the one whose node happened to trigger the start.

**What did you see instead?**

The receiver's logs node started before the traces pipeline's processor in around 20% of fresh builds (and after it the rest of the time), so the cross-signal order really does go both ways.
Within a single subgraph it's always fine — a receiver never starts before its own processor, and that assertion in the test never trips — so the risk is entirely from the other signal's node, which has no ordering relationship to `proc[traces]` at all.
Add the shared server coming up the instant that first node starts, and that's the `processor.go:202` nil deref.

**Environment**

- collector v0.153.0 / k8sattributesprocessor v1.59.0.
- Related: [contrib #47672][contrib-47672] (the panic), [core #12717][core-12717] (start order).

[contrib-47672]: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/47672
[core-12717]: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/12717


### Collector version

v0.153.0

### Environment information

Compiler(if manually compiled): (e.g., "go 14.2")

prompt.pr_title: [service] Start receivers after every other component type
prompt.pr_body:
#### Description

This PR constrains the start order of components so that receivers only start after every other type of component has started across all pipelines. Note that this is still reverse topological order, but with some of the free parameters fixed.

This avoids startup issues with pipelines like this:
```
receiver/1 → exporter/1
receiver/2 → exporter/2
```
in which `receiver/1` and `receiver/2` are two instances of a `sharedcomponent`.

Since `receiver/1` and `exporter/2` are in disconnected parts of the component graph, their order in the startup schedule is undefined, so the service might (depending on the hash of the component instance identities) decide to start `receiver/1` before `exporter/2`. But since starting `receiver/1` also starts `receiver/2`, which the service has no knowledge of, there is a chance for `receiver/2` to emit data to an unstarted `exporter/2`, which violates the standard component lifecycle.

#### Link to tracking issue
Fixes #15485

#### Testing
I added a unit test in `graph_test.go` which checks that a shared receiver which eagerly sends data on startup does not send data to an unstarted exporter. This test fails with the previous code in `graph.go`.

#### Authorship

- [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

issue.title: Support Windows named pipes as a transport in confignet
issue.body:
### Component(s)

config/confignet

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

It's often convenient to interact with collector components over a local network. Binding to ports on localhost is a solution, but can be troublesome - they're a global namespace of limited size, and are frequently gated behind a security boundary. IPC mechanisms which expose a network-like API, such as unix domain sockets, are much more convenient. The `confignet` already supports these, leveraging support from the Go stdlib.

Unix domain sockets are even supported on modern Windows versions. However, `confignet` lacks support for a Windows-native IPC mechanism that can be used this way.  

### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like to add support for Windows [named pipes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/ipc/named-pipes) as a transport in `confignet`. Named pipes aren't exactly semantically equivalent to unix domain sockets, but they're close enough for our purposes. They can be used to implement a server/client architecture passing around messages of raw bytes.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I looked at other Windows IPC mechanisms, but none of the others map cleanly onto `net.Conn`. Named pipes, on the other hand, are frequently and idiomatically used this way.

### Additional context

In terms of implementation, we can use microsoft's official library: https://github.com/microsoft/go-winio. I created an example implementation in this PR: .
